content.headline: Spain votes Sunday with Sánchez seeking to defy polls and block a rightward turn
content.shortHeadline: Spain votes as Sánchez seeks to defy polls and block a rightward turn
content.standfirst: The prime minister says he is confident of holding on, but the conservative People’s Party leads in the polls and may need support from Vox. The result could shift one of Europe’s largest economies to the right.

image.caption: Pedro Sánchez and his rivals made their final appeals to voters before Sunday’s election.

sources.originalTitle: Spanish PM and rivals rally supporters in final pitch for votes

segments.body: Spain’s party leaders have made their final appeals before Sunday’s election. Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez says he can defy the polls, while conservative rival Alberto Núñez Feijóo has promised a new era of “truth, decency and good governance”. The People’s Party is narrowly ahead, but may need the anti-immigration Vox party to govern.

segments.title: A close contest, with Vox in the balance
segments.body: Feijóo says he wants a majority, but has left open the prospect of agreements with Vox, whose leader Santiago Abascal held a rally in Valencia. Vox is seeking to nearly double its 33 seats. Sánchez and his left-wing ally Ada Colau urged supporters to keep Spain moving forward, while housing, immigration and corruption featured prominently in the campaign.

content.headline: Turkey arrests nine connected to opposition channel Halk TV, its owner says
content.shortHeadline: Nine connected to Turkey’s Halk TV arrested, owner says
content.standfirst: The channel’s London-based owner says relatives were among those detained, rejecting allegations of wrongdoing. The arrests follow a raid, state takeover and appointment of a new administrator at the pro-opposition broadcaster.

image.caption: Halk TV owner Cafer Mahiroğlu says Turkish authorities have destroyed the broadcaster.

sources.originalTitle: Turkish officials 'destroyed' pro-opposition TV channel, owner tells BBC

segments.body: Nine people connected to Halk TV have been arrested on charges including money laundering, bribery and spreading misleading information, the channel’s owner Cafer Mahiroğlu told the BBC. He said several relatives were among those detained and described the allegations against him and the broadcaster as “completely wrong”.

segments.title: Wider pressure on opposition media
segments.body: Prosecutors said two former Halk TV news anchors were among those detained and accused them of producing false reports in exchange for money. An arrest warrant has also been issued for news coordinator Kürşad Oğuz, whom prosecutors say is abroad. The channel’s headquarters were raided last month, broadcasts halted and a government-appointed administrator installed.

content.headline: Ukraine’s Zelensky says Trump is not pressing Russia hard enough for peace
content.shortHeadline: Zelensky says Trump is not pressing Russia hard enough
content.standfirst: In a BBC interview, Ukraine’s president criticises Donald Trump’s description of Vladimir Putin as a friend and says delays to US missile deliveries are costing lives. Kyiv faces another winter of attacks on infrastructure.

image.caption: Volodymyr Zelensky criticises Donald Trump’s relationship with Vladimir Putin in a BBC interview.

sources.originalTitle: Zelensky criticises 'strange' Trump-Putin friendship in BBC interview
Weary of war but with no sign of backing down, Kyiv faces another punishing winter

segments.body: Volodymyr Zelensky has criticised Donald Trump for calling Vladimir Putin “my friend”, saying the Russian president is an aggressor and “cannot be a friend”. In an interview with the BBC, Zelensky said the US was not pressing Moscow hard enough in peace talks and that it was unclear whether European negotiators would take part in the next round, expected in December.

segments.title: Missile defence and a hard winter
segments.body: Zelensky said Ukraine lacked enough interceptors for ballistic missiles and that delays to US Patriot deliveries were costing lives. He said Ukraine could destroy about 70% of Russia’s fastest drones, but described the shortage of missiles as “very, very big”. Russian strikes have hit power stations and bridges as Kyiv braces for winter.

perspectives.body: A BBC correspondent reporting from Kyiv describes dark nights, frequent air alerts and residents coping with power and water disruption. A poll cited in the report found 62% of Ukrainians prepared to endure the war for as long as necessary.

content.headline: China’s growing influence is making it harder for dissidents to be heard
content.shortHeadline: Dissidents say China’s influence is drowning out their voices
content.standfirst: Uyghur and Tibetan activists say international attention and support are fading as Beijing’s economic clout grows. Exiles also describe pressure around family visits, though China rejects claims that it seeks information or influence from them.

image.caption: Uyghur and Tibetan activists say China’s growing influence is pushing their concerns out of view.

sources.originalTitle: Behind China's spectacular rise, voices who defied it say they are being drowned out

segments.body: Uyghur activist Dolkun Isa says it has become harder to mobilise support for protests about China’s treatment of Uyghurs: he recalls thousands attending demonstrations in 2018, compared with difficulty finding 500 today. Activists interviewed by the BBC say human rights concerns are increasingly competing with economic interests and geopolitical calculations.

segments.title: Family ties and pressure in exile
segments.body: Uyghur and Tibetan activists say offers of family visits and contact with relatives can leave exiles fearful of speaking out or suspicious of people who return. Some describe feeling pressured to promote favourable accounts of China. Beijing’s UK embassy rejects claims that returnees are asked to spy or disclose information, saying family visits are a normal consular service.

content.headline: US storms leave more than 260,000 without power and disrupt holiday travel
content.shortHeadline: US storms leave 260,000 without power and disrupt travel
content.standfirst: Power outages and flight disruption continued after severe weather hit both coasts during Thanksgiving. Forecasters say conditions are improving in the north-east, but another system could bring heavy rain and strong winds on Monday.

image.caption: Floodwater and storm damage disrupted roads and travel across the United States over Thanksgiving.

sources.originalTitle: Hundreds of thousands still without power a day after US slammed with Thanksgiving storms

segments.body: More than 260,000 people remained without power Friday evening after severe weather brought high winds, heavy rain and coastal flooding to the eastern United States. Pennsylvania was the worst-hit state for outages. More than 3,400 flights were delayed and nearly 670 cancelled on Friday, following further disruption on Thanksgiving.

segments.title: Flooding and further disruption
segments.body: New York recorded its wettest Thanksgiving at Central Park, according to preliminary data, and the city’s Macy’s parade was postponed for the first time in its 100-year history. Flood warnings remained in parts of New Jersey. The storm is expected to move into eastern Canada, while another area of low pressure could bring more heavy rain and strong winds on Monday.

content.headline: Eight Peruvian military personnel killed in helicopter crash during rescue
content.shortHeadline: Eight killed in Peruvian military helicopter crash
content.standfirst: The pilot survived and was flown to Lima for treatment after the aircraft crashed during a mission in the remote VRAEM region. Authorities have not said what caused the crash.

image.caption: A Peruvian military helicopter crashed during a rescue mission in the country’s remote VRAEM region.

sources.originalTitle: Eight killed in Peruvian military helicopter crash

segments.body: Eight military personnel were killed when a helicopter crashed near Sanabamba in Peru’s VRAEM region, the defence ministry said. The pilot was the sole survivor and was evacuated to Lima for specialist treatment. The aircraft had been sent to evacuate an army patrol and was reported missing on Thursday night.

The crash occurred in a remote area known for coca cultivation and trafficking, where gangs and remnants of the Shining Path operate. Authorities have not given a cause for the crash or explained why the patrol needed rescuing. The military said the three personnel being evacuated were also among those killed.

content.headline: Swedish clinic reassesses ADHD and autism diagnoses, prompting concern from some
content.shortHeadline: Swedish clinic rechecks ADHD and autism diagnoses amid concerns
content.standfirst: A publicly funded clinic is offering reassessments to people who feel their diagnosis no longer fits, including those affected by career restrictions. Advocates warn that removing a diagnosis could deepen stigma or leave people without support.

image.caption: A Swedish clinic is reassessing people who feel their ADHD or autism diagnosis no longer fits.

sources.originalTitle: A clinic is reassessing people with ADHD and autism diagnoses - but critics fear it could deepen stigma

segments.body: A clinic in Sweden offers reassessments for people diagnosed with ADHD or autism who question whether the diagnosis still reflects their experience. Freya, whose name has been changed, sought a review after learning that an ADHD diagnosis could complicate her ambition to join the police. The clinic concluded that she did not currently meet the diagnostic criteria.

segments.title: A contested approach
segments.body: The clinic says it adds a new assessment to a person’s record rather than erasing the original diagnosis. But advocates warn that symptoms can return and that losing a diagnosis may make it harder to access timely support. Others argue that employment rules should change instead of putting pressure on individuals to seek reassessment. The clinic’s pilot study involved people already seeking to lose their diagnosis, so its results may not represent all people with ADHD or autism.

content.headline: Rodrigo Duterte’s ICC trial is set to examine killings in his war on drugs
content.shortHeadline: Duterte’s ICC trial will test accountability for his drug war
content.standfirst: The former Philippine president faces charges over alleged crimes against humanity when his trial opens on 30 November. The case could test the International Criminal Court’s ability to prosecute powerful leaders and give victims’ families a hearing.

image.caption: Former Philippine president Rodrigo Duterte is due to stand trial at the International Criminal Court.

sources.originalTitle: Why is former Philippine president Rodrigo Duterte on trial at The Hague?

segments.body: Former Philippine president Rodrigo Duterte is due to stand trial at the International Criminal Court in The Hague on 30 November, accused of crimes against humanity linked to his war on drugs. He faces three counts of murder and attempted murder covering events between 2011 and 2019. Duterte denies the allegations.

segments.title: A test for the court and the country
segments.body: The ICC says the cases will examine allegations that death squads targeted drug users and sellers. Human-rights monitors say the campaign disproportionately affected poor communities; estimates of the total deaths vary and the true toll is unknown. Families of some victims are expected to attend the opening. A final judgment could take years.

content.headline: DWP cyber incident leaves benefits and pensions services offline as claimants go
content.shortHeadline: DWP outage leaves claimants unable to access services
content.standfirst: The department says regular payments will continue and claimants will not be sanctioned for missed online journal entries. Some people report missing money or cancelled appointments; the cause of the incident remains unknown.

image.caption: The DWP says it is working with the National Cyber Security Centre as online services remain unavailable.

sources.originalTitle: DWP ‘cyber incident’ knocks almost all pensions and benefits systems offline
Millions lose access to benefits and pensions services after 'cyber incident'

segments.body: Many public-facing Department for Work and Pensions services remained offline on Friday after the department took its portal down following unusual activity. Claimants could not access services including Universal Credit, pension checks and disability-benefit applications. The DWP says regular benefit and pension payments are continuing and that no one will be sanctioned for missing online journal entries during the outage.

segments.title: Claimants report disruption
segments.body: Some claimants told the BBC they had not received expected payments and were worried about food, bills and job-search requirements; others reported cancelled appointments. The DWP urged people with urgent payment problems to contact its helpline and warned the public to watch for scams. Officials have not ruled out a malicious actor, but say there is no current evidence of customer data loss.

perspectives.body: The BBC spoke to claimants who described relying on expected payments for food and said they could not access online journals. The department said missed journal entries would not lead to sanctions while the incident is being dealt with.

content.headline: UK man jailed for 14 years for blackmailing girls in global cybercrime network
content.shortHeadline: Man jailed for blackmailing girls in global cybercrime network
content.standfirst: Beau-Jack Mensforth admitted coercing girls into self-harm and making indecent images. Victims described lasting trauma; police say the case highlights a wider online network targeting vulnerable young people.

image.caption: Beau-Jack Mensforth was jailed for 14 and a half years after admitting offences against girls.

sources.originalTitle: UK man jailed for online blackmail of vulnerable girls around the world
The Com: the global cybercrime network posing a ‘chilling threat’ to children

segments.body: Beau-Jack Mensforth, 20, was jailed for 14 and a half years after admitting 17 offences, including blackmail and making and distributing indecent images of children. A court heard he coerced girls around the world into self-harm, making images of themselves and harming pets. Victims described serious and lasting effects.

segments.title: A wider online threat
segments.body: Mensforth was part of the Com, a fluid network of young cybercriminals, according to police and the FBI. The Guardian reports that the UK National Crime Agency recorded a sixfold rise in reports linked to Com networks between 2022 and 2024. Northumbria police urged parents to talk with children and monitor changes in their online behaviour.

perspectives.body: The Guardian’s wider examination describes the Com as an international ecosystem involved in varied cybercrime, not only the abuse and blackmail in Mensforth’s case. It cites the FBI’s estimate that thousands identify as current or recent members.

content.headline: Labour MPs press Burnham over whether to approve Rosebank oilfield
content.shortHeadline: Labour MPs split over Rosebank as Burnham faces decision
content.standfirst: Supporters say the North Sea project would protect jobs and industry in Scotland; opponents cite its climate impact and limited contribution to UK energy supplies. The energy secretary will decide after a quasi-judicial process.

image.caption: Climate activists have urged the government to reject the Rosebank oilfield proposal.

sources.originalTitle: Labour row over Rosebank deepens as dozens of MPs warn PM not to block oilfield

segments.body: Labour is divided over whether to allow the Rosebank oilfield to proceed, with dozens of MPs pressing Prime Minister Andy Burnham to back it. Scottish Labour leader Michael Marra says jobs and livelihoods in the North Sea supply chain are at stake. Opponents say the project would produce an estimated 254m tonnes of carbon dioxide over its lifetime.

segments.title: A decision with political and climate stakes
segments.body: The Guardian reports that the field could generate an estimated £500m in tax receipts and 500 jobs, while critics argue it would add little to UK energy supplies. Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh is understood to be leaning against approval, but many MPs believe Burnham’s position could shape the outcome. Downing Street says the energy secretary will decide after considering the evidence and consultation responses.

content.headline: England’s flu season starts early as health officials urge eligible people to
content.shortHeadline: Flu admissions rise early as officials urge vaccination
content.standfirst: Hospital admissions for flu in England rose sharply in the latest weekly data, several weeks earlier than last season’s already early surge. Scientists say an early start does not necessarily mean a worse season overall.

sources.originalTitle: Why so many people are ill right now

segments.body: Flu admissions in England rose to 9.0 per 100,000 people last week, from 4.9 in the equivalent week last year, according to the UK Health Security Agency. The season began in October, and health officials say the increase is arriving earlier than in recent years. The NHS is urging everyone eligible to take up the flu vaccine.

segments.title: Early does not always mean worse
segments.body: Scientists say several factors may affect when flu peaks, including changes in circulating strains, weather and how people mix indoors. An early start does not on its own predict a worse season: last year also began early but overall activity later fell below average. Officials say vaccination remains the best protection against serious flu illness.

content.headline: Schools in England expected to set aside time for reading under proposed reforms
content.shortHeadline: England schools to set aside time for pupils to read for pleasure
content.standfirst: Education Secretary Lucy Powell is expected to outline curriculum changes on Monday, including daily reading time in primary schools and several sessions a week in secondary schools. A year 8 reading test is also proposed.

image.caption: Proposed curriculum reforms would give pupils in England regular time to read books and other literature.

sources.originalTitle: Schools in England must set aside time for pupils to read for pleasure

segments.body: Schools in England are expected to be required to give pupils time to read for pleasure under proposed curriculum reforms. Primary schools would set aside time each day, while secondary schools would do so several days a week. Education Secretary Lucy Powell is expected to announce the measures to Parliament on Monday.

The proposals also include a statutory reading test for year 8 pupils and a greater emphasis in secondary schools on reading whole books and poems. The government says it wants to address falling literacy and screen use. A survey cited by the National Literacy Trust found that reading enjoyment among young people was at its lowest level in two decades.

content.headline: Captain Tom Moore family charity applies to be struck off after watchdog report
content.shortHeadline: Captain Tom Moore’s family charity applies to be struck off
content.standfirst: The foundation, now renamed the 1189808 Foundation, has applied to be removed from the Companies House register. The move follows findings of repeated misconduct and mismanagement by the veteran’s daughter and her husband.

image.caption: Captain Sir Tom Moore and his daughter Hannah Ingram-Moore outside their home in 2020.

sources.originalTitle: Charity set up by Captain Tom Moore’s family applies to be struck off

segments.body: A charity established by the family of Captain Sir Tom Moore has applied to be struck off the Companies House register. The organisation dropped Moore’s name last year and is now called the 1189808 Foundation. The application appeared on the register on Friday.

The Charity Commission previously found a repeated pattern of misconduct and mismanagement by Hannah and Colin Ingram-Moore, including private financial gains through family links to the foundation. Both resigned as trustees and were barred from charity roles. The funds Moore raised for NHS Charities Together before the foundation was formed were not part of the regulator’s inquiry.

content.headline: OnlineCity cyberattack exposes data at Danish schools, car group and scout corps
content.shortHeadline: OnlineCity breach hits schools, car group and scout corps
content.standfirst: A supplier says attackers accessed and extracted data from its systems. More than 15,000 students’ phone numbers were exposed, while Semler Group says about 90,000 numbers and associated first names were compromised; the full scope is still unknown.

image.caption: OnlineCity.io, which provides bulk SMS services, has confirmed a cyberattack affecting customer data.

source.credit: Foto: Mads Claus Rasmussen / Ritzau Scanpix

sources.originalTitle: Teleudbyder bekræfter cyberangreb – flere er ramt
Tusindvis af gymnasieelevers telefonnumre er blevet lækket
Over 15.000 gymnasieelevers telefonnumre lækket
90.000 telefonnumre hos dansk bilkoncern er kompromitteret i stort sikkerhedsbrud

segments.body: OnlineCity.io has confirmed a cyberattack in which unauthorised people accessed and extracted data from its systems, including SMS traffic. The breach exposed 15,338 phone numbers linked to students at 23 upper-secondary schools. The school group says the attackers also accessed message sender IDs, send times and the first 20 characters of each SMS, including some messages sent through its “Secret Class” service.

segments.title: More organisations may be affected
segments.body: Semler Group says around 90,000 phone numbers and associated first names were compromised through the same supplier. The Danish Scout Association says 53 of its groups were affected. OnlineCity says the unauthorised access has been closed, but the total scope has not been established. Authorities have urged other organisations using the service to check whether they are affected.

perspectives.body: Semler Group says the exposed data includes phone numbers and first names, and warns customers to be alert to unexpected calls or messages seeking codes or payment details.

content.headline: Velkommen insolvency administrators tell police of concerns over customer debts
content.shortHeadline: Velkommen administrators alert police over suspected misconduct
content.standfirst: The collapsed energy group owed about 292 million kroner to nearly 43,000 customers, administrators say. They are examining company transactions and believe the former management may be liable for losses.

image.caption: Customers sought refunds at the Velkommen headquarters before the company collapsed.

sources.originalTitle: Elselskab skyldte elkunder 292 millioner ved konkurs – kuratorer har orienteret politiet
Politiet indblandet: Kuratorer mener, elselskab skyldte kunder 292 millioner ved konkurs

segments.body: Administrators of the collapsed Velkommen energy group say the companies owed about 292 million kroner to 42,825 customers when they went bankrupt. They have sent police a preliminary notification about matters found during their review and believe the former management may face compensation claims for continuing operations when losses were mounting.

segments.title: Where did the money go?
segments.body: The administrators say the group stopped returning customer prepayments from around 2024. They have identified large transfers and invoices between Velkommen and connected companies that require further investigation. The estate has assets of about 27 million kroner, while creditor claims exceed 600 million. One former director is believed to have left Denmark after administrators sought to restrict his travel.

perspectives.body: DR reports the administrators’ account of deleted emails and reset phones before they obtained them, as well as their current demand for 200 million kroner from former management. The precise destination of the customers’ money remains unresolved.

content.headline: Calls grow for state intervention after Kerteminde rejects Odense harbour plan
content.shortHeadline: Calls for state role after Kerteminde rejects harbour expansion
content.standfirst: Kerteminde’s council has halted work on a proposed two-billion-kroner expansion of Odense Harbour. Supporters warn of consequences for jobs and energy production, while opponents have raised concerns about nature and local communities.

image.caption: Opponents celebrated after Kerteminde’s council rejected further planning for the harbour expansion.

sources.originalTitle: Havnedrama afgjort: 'Nu skal vi hjem og have champagne'
13 byrødder har bremset kæmpe havneudvidelse - nu vil flere have staten på banen

segments.body: Kerteminde’s council has rejected further planning work for Odense Harbour’s proposed expansion, which would add about one million square metres, a deeper shipping channel and space for green-energy production. The harbour says more land is needed to meet demand. Local opponents celebrated the decision after years of campaigning.

segments.title: Supporters seek a national response
segments.body: Business representatives and politicians from neighbouring Odense say the project is too important to stop without further examination. They point to jobs, exports and the energy transition and want the state to consider stepping in. Opponents cited nature, nearby towns and the harbour’s relationship with local residents. The project’s future is uncertain.

content.headline: Denmark plans to bar prosecutors from wearing religious and political symbols
content.shortHeadline: Denmark to restrict prosecutors’ religious and political symbols
content.standfirst: The justice minister has asked prosecutors to issue new neutrality guidelines for court appearances. A law student who wears a headscarf says the change ends her ambition to become a prosecutor; a defence lawyer supports the restriction.

image.caption: Law student Imaan Fatima Shaheen says the planned guidelines threaten her ambition to become a prosecutor.

sources.originalTitle: Jurastuderendes drøm om at blive anklager ”er knust”

segments.body: Justice Minister Nicolai Wammen has asked the director of public prosecutions to issue guidelines requiring public prosecutors to appear religiously and politically neutral in court. The rules are expected to take effect “as soon as possible”. Imaan Fatima Shaheen, a law student who wears a headscarf, says the decision has put her career ambition out of reach.

segments.title: Disagreement over neutrality
segments.body: Shaheen argues that a headscarf does not prevent her from acting objectively and says the rule will especially affect women who wear one. Defence lawyer Erbil Kaya supports the restriction, arguing that prosecutors, like judges, must appear neutral to the public. It remains unclear how the guidelines will be applied in practice.

content.headline: TV 2 says it will assist police after being charged over The Black Swan
content.shortHeadline: TV 2 to assist police after being charged over documentary
content.standfirst: The broadcaster has not disclosed what it is charged with, and police have declined to specify the allegations. TV 2’s leaders say they stand by the documentary while taking the case seriously.

image.caption: TV 2 says it will cooperate with police in the investigation connected to The Black Swan.

source.credit: Foto: Mads Claus Rasmussen / Ritzau Scanpix

sources.originalTitle: TV 2 vil bistå politiet i opklaringsarbejde om Den sorte svane
TV 2 vil bistå politiet i opklaringsarbejde om Den sorte svane

segments.body: TV 2 says it will assist police in their investigation after being charged in connection with the 2024 documentary The Black Swan. Fyn Police have confirmed the charge but have not said what it concerns. TV 2’s board chair says the broadcaster takes the matter seriously, while its chief executive says she stands by publication of the programme.

segments.title: Questions about how the film was made
segments.body: The reporting says newspapers have previously disclosed that a legal academic warned TV 2 before publication about risks arising from a fake office set up during the project. The outlets also reported that the team gave a subject more than 1,000 pages of confidential case files, which TV 2 later apologised for. The charge itself remains unspecified.

perspectives.body: TV 2 says the documentary exposed serious crime and that those revelations remain sound. The broadcaster has not confirmed the specific allegations reported elsewhere and says it will wait for the authorities’ assessment.

content.headline: Danish YouTube duo’s company faces proposed fine over marketing to children
content.shortHeadline: YouTube duo’s company faces 140,000-kroner marketing fine
content.standfirst: The Consumer Ombudsman alleges that Mikkel and Emil Trier Pedersen’s company used hidden advertising and urged children to buy merchandise. The brothers deny wrongdoing; judgment is due on 4 December.

image.caption: Mikkel and Emil Trier Pedersen outside court, where their company faces a marketing-law case.

sources.originalTitle: Kendte Youtube-brødre risikerer bøde på 140.000 kroner

segments.body: TrendTube ApS, the company run by YouTube twins Mikkel and Emil Trier Pedersen, is accused of breaching Denmark’s marketing law in videos aimed at children. The Consumer Ombudsman says the videos included hidden advertising and encouraged young viewers to buy merchandise. The company appeared in court on Friday.

The Consumer Ombudsman has proposed a fine of 140,000 kroner, arguing that children are particularly vulnerable consumers. The brothers say they are shocked by the case and want to be acquitted, noting that the allegations concern four videos out of about 3,000. A judgment is due on 4 December.

content.headline: Ireland beat Australia 38-14 to finish November with four wins
content.shortHeadline: Ireland beat Australia 38-14 in autumn finale
content.standfirst: Ireland recovered from a slow start to beat Australia in London, securing fifth place in the inaugural Nations Championship and completing a clean sweep of their four November Tests.

image.caption: Ireland beat Australia 38-14 in London.

sources.originalTitle: Five-try Ireland beat Australia in autumn finale

segments.body: Australia took an early lead, but Ireland scored 24 unanswered points either side of half-time to take control. James McNabney scored twice in the closing seven minutes as Andy Farrell’s side finished with a comfortable 38-14 win.

segments.title: A strong end to the year
segments.body: The victory means Ireland won all four of their November Tests, including last week’s 20-17 win over South Africa. They finish 2026 with 10 wins and two defeats from 12 internationals.

content.headline: Forest beat Chelsea 3-2 as Gibbs-White scores twice
content.shortHeadline: Gibbs-White brace helps Forest beat Chelsea
content.standfirst: Igor Jesus opened the scoring with a volley before Morgan Gibbs-White struck twice for Nottingham Forest. Chelsea pulled back two goals but suffered a fourth defeat in five matches.

image.caption: Nottingham Forest beat Chelsea 3-2 at the City Ground.

sources.originalTitle: Gibbs-White stars, Fofana struggles - player ratings for Forest v Chelsea

segments.body: Forest beat Chelsea 3-2 at the City Ground. Igor Jesus volleyed in after five minutes, then Gibbs-White scored twice in the second half, including from the penalty spot. Emmanuel Emegha replied with two goals for Chelsea.

content.headline: Overton takes five as England beat Australia in third T20
content.shortHeadline: Overton’s five-wicket haul puts England 2-1 up
content.standfirst: Jamie Overton claimed his first international five-wicket haul as England bowled Australia out for 108 at The Gabba, then reached a rain-revised target to win by seven wickets.

image.caption: England have won 18 of 21 completed T20s this year.

sources.originalTitle: England outclass Aussies again to take series lead

segments.body: Overton took 5-12 and Liam Dawson 3-16 as Australia were dismissed for 108, their lowest total in a home T20. After three rain delays, England chased a revised target of 93, reaching it at 93-3 in 8.5 overs under the Duckworth-Lewis-Stern method.

segments.title: Overton makes his mark
segments.body: The win gives England a 2-1 lead in the five-match series. Overton said he had been disappointed with his bowling earlier on the tour and was pleased to produce a strong performance after extra work in training.

content.headline: Arsenal part company with head coach Renee Slegers
content.shortHeadline: Arsenal and Slegers part company after poor start
content.standfirst: Slegers leaves 18 months after leading Arsenal to the Women’s Champions League title. The club says results have fallen below expectations, with the side sixth in the WSL after 11 matches.

image.caption: Renee Slegers led Arsenal to the 2025 Women’s Champions League title.

sources.originalTitle: Head coach Slegers leaves Arsenal 18 months after Champions League win

segments.body: Arsenal and Renee Slegers have parted company by mutual consent. Assistant coach Aaron D’Antino has also left, while Melissa Clarke-Reed takes interim charge as the club searches for a permanent replacement.

segments.title: Results fall short
segments.body: Arsenal are sixth after 11 WSL matches, 12 points behind leaders Chelsea, and have gone four league games without a win. Director of women’s football Clare Wheatley said results were below the expected level and that change was necessary.

content.headline: Manchester United activate Bruno Fernandes’ contract extension
content.shortHeadline: United extend Fernandes’ deal to 2028
content.standfirst: Manchester United have activated the one-year option in their captain’s contract. Talks over a new deal are paused, while the extension protects the club’s ability to command a fee if he leaves.

image.caption: Bruno Fernandes joined Manchester United in 2020.

sources.originalTitle: Man Utd trigger Fernandes' one-year contract extension

segments.body: Fernandes’ contract was due to expire next summer, but the option extends it through to 2028. The Portugal international has made 343 appearances and scored 115 goals for United since joining in 2020.

segments.title: Long-term future remains open
segments.body: Discussions over a new contract have been paused and are expected to resume once United’s league position improves. Fernandes said earlier in the week that he remains ambitious to win the game’s biggest honours.

content.headline: Australia leave Nathan Lyon out of Test squad for New Zealand series
content.shortHeadline: Lyon omitted from Australia’s New Zealand squad
content.standfirst: The 39-year-old off-spinner is left out of Australia’s squad for four Tests, with selectors citing a lack of recent impact. The decision is not thought to be connected to the sandpaper controversy.

image.caption: Nathan Lyon played twice in Australia’s recent series defeat in South Africa.

sources.originalTitle: Australia drop Lyon for New Zealand Tests

segments.body: Lyon, who has 577 Test wickets, has been omitted from Australia’s squad for the series starting in Perth on 9 December. Uncapped off-spinner Corey Rocchiccioli is included, while Marnus Labuschagne also misses out.

segments.title: A significant selection call
segments.body: Chair of selectors George Bailey said Lyon had not had the impact Australia wanted in recent matches, while noting his experience could still be valuable. The report says the omission is not thought to be linked to the renewed sandpaper debate; Lyon has also struggled with form and fitness since 2023.

content.headline: Snooker players describe the sport’s toll on mental health
content.shortHeadline: Snooker’s mental strain—and the support available
content.standfirst: Mark Allen has spoken of being in a major low, while other players describe the isolation and pressure of the sport. The report examines existing support and calls for better awareness of it.

sources.originalTitle: Why snooker could be the most mentally challenging sport

segments.body: Allen has described a difficult period and said he was in a “major low”. The report does not establish what caused his struggles. It sets his experience alongside other players’ accounts of the solitude, long practice hours and public scrutiny that can accompany professional snooker.

segments.title: Support and its limits
segments.body: The WPBSA has partnered with Sporting Chance since 2021, providing more than 180 counselling sessions and access to a confidential helpline. Gary Wilson says players lower down the tour also struggle; he and others have suggested support at tournaments could make help easier to access.

content.headline: Musiala’s latest injury deepens Bayern’s questions over his future
content.shortHeadline: Musiala’s injury and health raise questions at Bayern
content.standfirst: Jamal Musiala has torn his right hamstring after a brief return, adding to a series of injuries as he manages absence seizures. Bayern’s public comments about his contract have also strained relations.

image.caption: Jamal Musiala came on as a substitute against Lille before his latest injury.

sources.originalTitle: What happens now for Bayern Munich and Musiala?

segments.body: Musiala is out until further notice after tearing his right hamstring. His comeback had lasted two appearances following recovery from another hamstring injury, a broken fibula and ankle problems. The report says he also has absence seizures, which require daily medication.

segments.title: Health and contract tensions
segments.body: Bayern supervisory board member Karl-Heinz Rummenigge publicly questioned Musiala’s salary in light of his health, prompting criticism from team-mate Joshua Kimmich and the players’ union Fifpro. Bayern later said a meeting with Musiala’s representatives had agreed that his health should come first.

segments.title: What remains unknown
segments.body: The report says there is no evidence that Musiala’s 2025 car crash was caused by a seizure, or that it caused his condition. His recovery and whether the damage to his relationship with Bayern can be repaired remain unresolved.

content.headline: Phoebe Bridgers’ phone-free arena show turns private grief into a shared release
content.shortHeadline: Phoebe Bridgers makes a phone-free arena feel intimate
content.standfirst: At Manchester’s Co-op Live, locked-away phones focused attention on a set shaped by grief and vulnerability. Two accounts find the restriction both inconvenient and unexpectedly freeing for the crowd and Bridgers alike.

image.caption: Phoebe Bridgers performs beneath the dome at Co-op Live in Manchester.

sources.originalTitle: Phoebe Bridgers review – phone-free arena show is a cosmic, communal revelation
Phoebe Bridgers’ controversial concert rule left me uneasy – but it was a revelation

segments.body: At a 23,000-capacity arena, the absence of glowing screens changes the feel of the room. The Guardian’s review describes Bridgers’ expansive, carefully staged show as a communal space where the crowd can attend to difficult songs rather than record them. Its emotional centre is “Still Standing”, her complex memorial to her father, met by audible sobbing.

segments.title: A different kind of attention
segments.body: The i’s reviewer also found the phone pouch frustrating before the show: it made checking a seat number and buying a drink harder, and raised concerns about communication in an emergency. Once the music began, though, the reviewer felt unusually absorbed—especially during “Still Standing”—and valued knowing the performance would not be turned into a stream of online clips.

perspectives.body: The i’s account gives the policy a practical counterpoint to the Guardian’s more atmospheric review: the inconvenience was real, but so was the relief of being present without checking or filming on a phone.

segments.title: The show behind the rule
segments.body: The Guardian describes the dome above the stage opening onto cosmic imagery, while Bridgers and her nine-piece band move from restrained arrangements to crashing crescendos. The crowd’s roar during “Motion Sickness” and the silence around her solo acoustic tribute suggest that the phone ban is not simply a restriction: it shapes the show’s movement between spectacle and closeness.

content.headline: Jennifer Reid carries the voices of Industrial Revolution workers into the world
content.shortHeadline: Jennifer Reid keeps working-class ballads alive
content.standfirst: The Manchester singer has learned hundreds of songs written by workers in Lancashire’s mills and mines. Her performances preserve their voices while drawing connections between industrial-era hardship and working conditions today.

image.caption: Jennifer Reid, who performs traditional workers’ songs from Lancashire.

sources.originalTitle: ‘I’m like a lamp-post. Not glam, but vital’: Jennifer Reid, the singer saving the Industrial Revolution’s working-class songs

segments.body: Jennifer Reid began collecting and learning local broadside ballads while volunteering at Chetham’s Library. She now tours with a repertoire of about 300 songs, many in Lancashire dialect, and teaches children about the history and oral traditions around them. Her first gig was a performance at the 2013 Venice Biennale, after she persuaded artist Jeremy Deller to give her a place.

segments.title: Preserving the old shape
segments.body: Reid describes her approach as preserving the material before reshaping it. She studies archival recordings and dialect, and practised clog dancing to bring the rhythms of mill work into performance. The songs, she says, were written by workers themselves—not by people looking back on their lives from a distance.

segments.title: Then and now
segments.body: A trip to Bangladesh sharpened the contemporary resonance for Reid: she says garment workers’ songs there were strikingly similar to Lancashire ballads, and workers described conditions that recalled those of nineteenth-century factories. She stresses that the Industrial Revolution’s history must be understood alongside colonialism and suffering, not softened into nostalgia.

content.headline: Echobelly return with a new album after Britpop’s upheavals and years apart
content.shortHeadline: Echobelly find freedom in their return
content.standfirst: Sonya Madan and Glenn Johansson look back on Britpop’s excesses and describe making Eye-magi-nation, their first album in nearly a decade. The duo say self-releasing it after a label dispute gave them new creative freedom.

image.caption: Sonya Madan and Glenn Johansson of Echobelly in 2026.

sources.originalTitle: ‘We had a drug dealer called Satan on our tour bus’: Britpop stars Echobelly on debauchery, being pals with Oasis – and their spiritual return

segments.body: Echobelly’s Sonya Madan and Glenn Johansson recall a close friendship with Oasis and a turbulent US tour in 1994, including a visitor they remember introducing himself on their bus as “Satan”, a local drug dealer. Their new album, Eye-magi-nation, is due next spring and follows nearly a decade without a record.

segments.title: Making music on their own terms
segments.body: The pair, now Echobelly’s only official members, say a two-year dispute with their label led them to self-release the album. Madan describes the process as creatively freeing, though far from glamorous: she says she recorded vocals in the bathroom and wrote songs in a wardrobe to avoid disturbing the neighbours.

segments.title: A scene remembered differently
segments.body: Madan disputes the idea that Britpop’s male musicians were generally sexist, saying she found them kind, while describing rivalry and a lack of solidarity among some female-fronted bands. She also recalls the pressure of being pitted against other women by music journalists. Her account complicates, rather than settles, the debate over how women experienced the scene.

content.headline: Lizabett Russo returns to Transylvania for a searching, shape-shifting folk set
content.shortHeadline: Lizabett Russo makes a folk album of longing
content.standfirst: On Pe Unde Trece Dorul, the Scottish-based singer learns songs in remote Romanian villages and threads them into spectral, contemporary arrangements. The review praises her range and the album’s striking shifts in sound.

image.caption: Singer Lizabett Russo, whose album draws on Romanian folk traditions.

sources.originalTitle: The month’s best folk album: Lizabett Russo confronts her roots on an odyssey through Transylvania

segments.body: For her fifth album, Lizabett Russo returned to Romania, where she grew up, and travelled through Transylvania to learn traditional songs and calls. Its title, roughly translated as Where Longing Goes, comes from a song taught to her by farmer Maria Dulău, recognised as a Living Human Treasure by Romania’s National Institute of Heritage.

segments.title: Tradition in motion
segments.body: The review hears an album that moves between layered vocals, kaval, guitar and cello, with Russo’s voice shifting from gentle agility to an eerie a cappella delivery. Its centrepiece, “Dragă Mi-o Fost Lumea Mie”, builds from tender instrumentation into discordance, pauses for deep breaths, then returns to Russo’s voice.

segments.title: Other new folk records
segments.body: The review also recommends A Wild Inhabitation, a collaboration by Antoni O’Breskey and his daughter Consuelo Nerea Breschi; Claire Cronin’s spare, uncanny The Bruise; and Craven’s The Fruits of Idleness, Disgrace, and Death, which it calls a spirited collection.

content.headline: Morten Harket reflects on Parkinson’s, fame and a-ha’s early struggles
content.shortHeadline: Morten Harket on Parkinson’s and life beyond fame
content.standfirst: The a-ha frontman says his Parkinson’s diagnosis changed his access to singing and guitar, but also brought a new appreciation for the body. In a reader Q&A, he revisits early hardship, songwriting and the cost of sudden fame.

image.caption: a-ha frontman Morten Harket.

sources.originalTitle: a-ha’s Morten Harket: ‘My Parkinson’s diagnosis wasn’t devastating. I have a new appreciation for the human organism’

segments.body: Morten Harket says medication side-effects have affected his access to singing and guitar, and that the diagnosis forced him to reassemble his sense of self. He describes it not as devastating, but as a reason to appreciate the body’s complexity. For Human Grace, his new album, he and his collaborators drew on older recordings of his voice.

segments.title: The view from the early days
segments.body: Harket remembers a-ha’s first years in south London as exciting but precarious: the group lacked money and shared limited sleeping space in poor conditions. He says he never doubted the band would succeed, even when his bandmates were less certain, and recalls fame as a sudden, profound loss of ordinary life.

segments.title: A continuing search
segments.body: The answers range from memories of writing and faith to a reflection on what he thinks younger people seek: belonging and human connection. Harket says curiosity has remained central to him, even as he has become more sceptical about the world’s leaders and their willingness to take responsibility.

content.headline: Liz Harris lets the sounds of rivers flow through two film scores
content.shortHeadline: Grouper’s Liz Harris finds music in water
content.standfirst: Music for Two Films About Water gathers Liz Harris’s scores for films by Tanja Engelberts and Takashi Makino. The review finds a lovely, if mostly instrumental, meeting of her ambient sensibility and the recordings of water themselves.

sources.originalTitle: Music for Two Films About Water

segments.body: Liz Harris, best known as Grouper, collects music for two short films on her first release under her own name. For Tanja Engelberts’ We Exhale, recordings of the Rhône River are woven into the composition, so the water’s changing volume helps map the spaces the film travels through.

segments.title: A quieter current
segments.body: The score for Takashi Makino’s Constellation is more static, mostly piano suspended in water sounds. The review says keeping the films’ recorded audio within the music connects with Harris’s history of working alongside experimental filmmakers, while noting that the album’s mostly instrumental textures give less room to the layered vocals that are among her strengths.

content.headline: Thoom turns hyperpop’s digital gloss into an expressive blend of Arabic sounds
content.shortHeadline: Thoom makes hyperpop intimate and ferocious
content.standfirst: On her debut, Los Angeles-based Zeynab Marwan combines hyperpop production with Arabic instrumentation and a forceful, shifting vocal style. The review finds the album most compelling when personal feeling and cultural identity meet.

sources.originalTitle: Everyday, Everything Is at Stake

segments.body: Zeynab Marwan, who records as Thoom, draws on hyperpop, Arabic instrumentation and the theatrical pull of Lebanese pop. Her debut, Everyday, Everything Is at Stake, was made with producers including Dylan Brady and Ike Clateman, and places her voice—by turns melodic, smoky and aggressive—at the front of the mix.

segments.title: Intensity with a sense of place
segments.body: The review highlights the pounding mizmar drone of “Janani”, the slow-burn warning in “Morocco” and the restless heartbreak of “Adfil”. Its final track, “I’m Going Back to Lebanon”, joins the pain of leaving a lover to uncertainty about returning home, asking whether the summer has ended and whether there is war again.

content.headline: Aphex Twin’s Drukqs still tests the boundaries between club music and concert-h,
content.shortHeadline: Aphex Twin’s Drukqs, 25 years on
content.standfirst: A new anniversary edition revives Richard D. James’s sprawling 2001 album, where breakbeats, prepared piano and electronic experimentation coexist. The review argues that its unruly scale is central to its achievement.

sources.originalTitle: Drukqs (25th Anniversary Edition)

segments.body: Twenty-five years after its release, Drukqs remains a 100-minute collision of Aphex Twin’s rhythmic ingenuity and a new interest in prepared piano. The review sees it as a bridge between electronic music’s club traditions and the more academic experiments of the concert hall, rather than a retreat from the dancefloor.

segments.title: Precision and excess
segments.body: On “54 Cymru Beats”, fast, intricate drums approach the point where rhythm blurs into pitch. Elsewhere, programmed Disklavier pieces turn an acoustic piano into something both mechanical and delicate. The album’s length and sharp shifts can be tiring, but the review argues that its apparent incoherence reflects music continually straining against boundaries.

content.headline: Mike Leigh says worsening myositis means Tender Loving Care will be his last
content.shortHeadline: Mike Leigh says his latest film will be his last
content.standfirst: After 55 years of filmmaking, the 83-year-old director says his worsening myositis has made the physical demands of directing impossible. He is not retiring, but regrets that he never made the big-budget contemporary film he wanted.

image.caption: Director Mike Leigh, whose latest film is expected to be his last.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Everybody tells me how I can keep working. My answer begins with ‘F’ and ends with ‘off’: Mike Leigh on 55 years of films – and why he’s just made his last

segments.body: Mike Leigh says Tender Loving Care, his 17th feature, is likely to be his last. His myositis has weakened his muscles and restricted his movement; he says directing has become physically beyond him, though he still intends to write. He had not realised during the film’s production that it would be his final one.

segments.title: A way of making films
segments.body: Leigh describes his long-established process as months of rehearsal and improvisation with actors, gradually distilled into precise scenes. He says he has never wanted a film to be a vehicle for a star, arguing that the expectation to cast big names can distract from the work and its collaborative development.

segments.title: The film he could not make
segments.body: Leigh says his lasting regret is that he could not secure backing for a large-scale contemporary story about friends from different ethnic and racial backgrounds, told across generations. A producer suggested developing it as television, but the BBC rejected the proposal. His latest film follows two social workers and the people around them, trying to care for one another in modern London.

content.headline: A Hollywood set builder turns cabin interiors into convincing in-flight scenes
content.shortHeadline: The specialist sets behind Hollywood’s airplane scenes
content.standfirst: Richard Chan’s Aero Mock-Ups supplies plane cabins, cockpits and details for films and television, from Bridesmaids to Focker-in-Law. The former pilot explains how an aviation salvage business became a niche part of Hollywood production.

image.caption: Aero Mock-Ups’ airplane-cabin set used in Focker-in-Law.

sources.originalTitle: Get me a 747 and deploy the oxygen masks! The British pilot behind Hollywood’s greatest inflight scenes

segments.body: When a film needs an airplane cabin, a cockpit or oxygen masks that really deploy, it may turn to Aero Mock-Ups, a Hollywood-based specialist run by British former pilot Richard Chan. Its work has appeared in films including Bridesmaids and Inception, as well as television series from Grey’s Anatomy to Westworld.

segments.title: From aircraft salvage to film sets
segments.body: Chan began collecting aircraft interiors and parts through his aviation work, initially intending to strip a Boeing cabin for salvage. A former secretary with experience as a script supervisor suggested showing it to production people; the cabin led to his first television job, and then to a business supplying detailed airline interiors and props.

segments.title: More than a film prop
segments.body: Aero Mock-Ups has also helped cabin crews and other teams practise safety procedures, and supplied a sensory room at San Francisco International Airport for travellers who are neurodivergent, anxious about flying or unfamiliar with air travel. Chan hopes to expand the warehouses into an airport set where a production can film from check-in through to boarding.

content.headline: You Can See Everything blurs the line between documentary and performance
content.shortHeadline: The reality games inside You Can See Everything
content.standfirst: The film’s staged intimacy with Elizabeth Holmes raises questions about truth, sympathy and the filmmaker’s role. One review sees a troublingly generous portrait; another traces its hall-of-mirrors approach to Abbas Kiarostami’s Close-Up.

image.caption: Elizabeth Holmes in You Can See Everything.

sources.originalTitle: Elizabeth Holmes is not the villain of You Can See Everything. That’s a problem
You Can See Everything overtly riffs on Vertigo. But how big is its debt to Kiarostami’s Close-Up?

segments.body: Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s You Can See Everything follows Elizabeth Holmes before she begins her prison sentence, with Fielder and a crew moving into her family’s life. The i’s review finds the result unsettling and engrossing, but says its domestic portrait leaves the viewer with a more sympathetic impression of Holmes than the reviewer expected.

segments.title: Who is directing whom?
segments.body: The Guardian connects the film’s mix of real people, reconstruction and performance to Abbas Kiarostami’s Close-Up, in which a man impersonates filmmaker Mohsen Makhmalbaf and Kiarostami inserts himself into the story. Co-director Oppenheim has named Close-Up as a favourite film. The comparison highlights how both works make it difficult to decide what is being staged and what is real.

perspectives.body: The i’s review focuses on the ethical risk of the film’s closeness: as Holmes is shown as a wife and mother, the documentary may invite sympathy while leaving the viewer unsure whether she is sincere or still managing the story.

segments.title: A question without an easy answer
segments.body: For The i, the uncertainty becomes particularly sharp after Holmes enters prison and Fielder’s attention shifts to her husband, Billy Evans. The reviewer argues that Evans’s behaviour threatens to displace Holmes as the subject of her own story, while leaving open the question of how much Holmes understands or participates in the film’s unfolding performance.

content.headline: Minotaur turns a Russian businessman’s corruption into wartime noir
content.shortHeadline: A Russian mini-oligarch in wartime noir
content.standfirst: Andrey Zvyagintsev’s first film in almost a decade follows a provincial businessman asked to supply workers for Russia’s war in Ukraine. The review finds a thriller about infidelity and violence whose political context sharpens its portrait of moral cowardice.

image.caption: A scene from Andrey Zvyagintsev’s Minotaur.

sources.originalTitle: Minotaur review – Andrey Zvyagintsev’s scorching noir intrigue amid the Ukraine war

segments.body: In Andrey Zvyagintsev’s Minotaur, businessman Gleb is told that local firms must provide men for military call-up without disrupting the economy. He devises a scheme to recruit truck drivers on false promises of high pay, knowing they will be sent to war before he has to pay them.

segments.title: Power and evasion
segments.body: Gleb’s private crisis—he suspects his wife Galina is unfaithful—runs alongside the public machinery of the war. The review reads the film’s plot of infidelity and revenge through its larger portrait of disillusionment, political bad faith and the ways powerful people cover up their own misdeeds.

segments.title: Violence as a lesson
segments.body: When Gleb’s son says he is being bullied, his father advises him to threaten the boy who is tormenting him. The review sees this as a poisonous education in violence, but also a telling contrast with Gleb’s own cowardly, concealed schemes. Dmitriy Mazurov and Iris Lebedeva lead performances set against Zvyagintsev’s cold, crime-scene-like compositions.

content.headline: Avengers: Doomsday turns Marvel’s continuity into a puzzle for fans
content.shortHeadline: Marvel’s latest Avengers film comes with homework
content.standfirst: A new trailer appears to link Steve Rogers, the Fantastic Four and Doctor Doom through the MCU’s multiverse. The connections are still speculative, but the Guardian argues that piecing them together is part of the appeal for Marvel devotees.

image.caption: James Marsden as Cyclops in Avengers: Doomsday.

sources.originalTitle: Avengers: Doomsday has brought with it more ‘Marvel homework’ than ever. That’s just as it should be

segments.body: The latest Avengers: Doomsday trailer raises questions about the return of Chris Evans as Steve Rogers and the arrival of Pedro Pascal’s Reed Richards at his home. The Guardian considers whether Rogers and Peggy Carter might have moved to another reality, and whether that could connect to the threat posed by Doctor Doom.

segments.title: Clues for the committed
segments.body: The speculation draws on earlier films and series: Rogers’ time travel in Avengers: Endgame, Loki’s role in holding the multiverse together, and the incursions described in Endgame: Encore. The article treats these connections as questions prompted by the trailer, not confirmed explanations, and argues that this kind of continuity-hunting is precisely what fans enjoy ahead of an Avengers release.

content.headline: The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth is a laid-back macho fantasy
content.shortHeadline: Cliff Booth returns in a languid Hollywood caper
content.standfirst: David Fincher directs Brad Pitt in Quentin Tarantino’s spin-off about his Once Upon a Time in Hollywood stuntman. The BBC review enjoys its 1970s Los Angeles detail but finds little story, depth or respect for characters beyond straight white men.

sources.originalTitle: The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth review: Brad Pitt returns to his Oscar-winning role in a 'macho fantasy' ★★★☆☆

segments.body: Brad Pitt returns as Cliff Booth in a spin-off scripted by Quentin Tarantino and directed by David Fincher. Set in Los Angeles in 1977, the film follows Cliff as he spends time at a cinema, mixes margaritas and occasionally uses his wartime experience to scare off crooks threatening his film-industry friends.

segments.title: Atmosphere over momentum
segments.body: The review enjoys the film’s vintage cars, landline phones and old cinemas, and praises Elizabeth Debicki and Scott Caan in supporting roles. But Cliff’s encounters take a long time to lead to the central criminal problem, leaving the film, in the reviewer’s view, with a thin plot and a rambling, anecdotal shape.

segments.title: An old-fashioned point of view
segments.body: The BBC calls the film an antiquated macho fantasy, arguing that it gives little attention to anyone who is not a straight white man. Its conclusion is that the collaboration between two ambitious filmmakers delivers an easy-to-watch nostalgia piece rather than the daring work either might have made.

content.headline: Josephine asks how to show sexual violence through a child’s eyes
content.shortHeadline: Josephine confronts sexual violence through a child’s eyes
content.standfirst: Beth de Araújo’s film follows an eight-year-old who witnesses a rape, drawing on the director’s own experience. Its unflinching opening has prompted debate over the ethics and purpose of showing sexual violence on screen.

sources.originalTitle: 'The subject is still taboo': Shocking new film Josephine confronts sexual violence through a child's eyes

segments.body: Josephine begins when its eight-year-old title character comes across a rape in San Francisco’s Golden Gate Park. The film follows the trauma’s effects on her and her parents. Director Beth de Araújo says the story draws on her own experience of witnessing the aftermath of a rape when she was a child.

segments.title: A difficult choice
segments.body: De Araújo says she wanted viewers to encounter the event from a child’s perspective, before the child fully understands what rape is. The film took precautions around its young lead, Mason Reeves: a child psychologist was available to her family, she did not read the script, and she has not seen the finished film.

segments.title: What the scene is doing
segments.body: The article sets Josephine against earlier screen depictions of rape, some criticised for centring the perpetrator or using assault as spectacle. Film scholar Tanya Horeck says there is no single feminist rulebook for such scenes, but finds a case for this one because it shapes the child’s trauma and the rest of the film.

content.headline: Mark Gatiss’s The Bride’s Chamber may be his best Ghost Story for Christmas yet
content.shortHeadline: A Ghost Story for Christmas delivers a new high
content.standfirst: Martin Freeman plays a Dickens-like author drawn into a tale of cruelty and remorse in Mark Gatiss’s latest festive ghost story. The review praises its playful approach, dark subject and genuinely frightening supernatural finish.

image.caption: Martin Freeman as Francis Goodchild in A Ghost Story for Christmas: The Bride’s Chamber.

sources.originalTitle: A Ghost Story for Christmas: The Bride’s Chamber review – Mark Gatiss just made his best spooky festive tale yet

segments.body: The Bride’s Chamber adapts a Charles Dickens story from 1857, with Martin Freeman as Francis Goodchild, a writer who strongly resembles Dickens, and Jim Broadbent as the ghost who tells him of a cruel man and the young wife he urges to die. The Guardian calls the result tremendous fun, with a dark story at its centre.

segments.title: A tradition with room to roam
segments.body: The review places Gatiss’s revival alongside the 1970s Ghost Story for Christmas adaptations, but argues that his run has become a high point in its own right. Rather than return to the series’ familiar M R James stories, Gatiss has recently drawn on writers including Arthur Conan Doyle, E Nesbit and E F Benson.

segments.title: No easy redemption
segments.body: Unlike A Christmas Carol, this is not a story of reform or a happy ending: the review describes it as a tale of a bad man living with the consequences of what he has done. Its final supernatural flourish is praised as genuinely frightening, and as a mark of how the series can still surprise.

content.headline: Blade Runner 2099 makes a haunting television world of memory and decay
content.shortHeadline: Blade Runner 2099 is all neon and unease
content.standfirst: Michelle Yeoh and Hunter Schafer lead the first television expansion of the Blade Runner story, where replicants hunt humans and memory has become contraband. The review praises its visual world while wishing for a firmer episodic shape.

image.caption: A scene from Blade Runner 2099.

sources.originalTitle: Blade Runner 2099 review – every scene of this TV version is packed with terrifying visual beauty

segments.body: Set 50 years after Blade Runner 2049, the series reverses the familiar hunt: blade runners are now replicants pursuing disobedient humans, while the capture and storage of human memories is illegal. Michelle Yeoh plays ageing blade runner Olwen; Hunter Schafer is Cora, a human passing as a replicant.

segments.title: A future built from images
segments.body: The Guardian says creator and writer Silka Luisa keeps the franchise’s future more atmospheric than neatly explained. The review revels in neon, shadows, abandoned spaces and a soundtrack of shimmering synths and soulful saxophone, describing a world where people try to cope as everything around them breaks down.

segments.title: An elliptical pursuit
segments.body: Olwen and Cora seek Olwen’s former colleague Marek, who appears to have gone rogue with a group of replicants. The review finds emotional force in their search for elusive memories, but says the series could have offered a stronger episodic structure without losing its strange, end-times mood.

content.headline: A new Pride and Prejudice joins TV’s long history of period drama
content.shortHeadline: The period dramas that still hold up
content.standfirst: As Dolly Alderton’s Netflix adaptation arrives, Guardian writers revisit the costume dramas that have endured—from Brideshead Revisited and Wolf Hall to The Crimson Petal and the White and Life on Mars.

image.caption: Emma Corrin as Elizabeth Bennet and Jack Lowden as Mr Darcy in Pride and Prejudice.

sources.originalTitle: Tighten your corsets! Pass the smelling salts! It’s the greatest period dramas ever made

segments.body: Dolly Alderton’s new Pride and Prejudice, starring Emma Corrin and Jack Lowden, offers a reason to revisit television’s long relationship with period drama. The Guardian’s writers pick favourites across settings and styles, from the lavish locations of Brideshead Revisited to the pressured romantic stakes of Andrew Davies’s earlier Austen adaptation.

segments.title: More than costumes
segments.body: The selection makes the case for period drama beyond bonnets and stately homes: Wolf Hall is praised for translating Hilary Mantel’s novels into intimate, layered television, while Mad Men uses its recent past to examine the gradual unravelling of social conventions. Life on Mars turns nostalgia for the 1970s into a question about memory and reality.

segments.title: Lives beyond the drawing room
segments.body: Other choices take in the working lives and constraints beneath period spectacle, including The Crimson Petal and the White, about a sex worker navigating Victorian London, and a drama about the Brontë sisters’ struggle to publish and earn a living. The list also highlights queer history in Tipping the Velvet.

content.headline: Sweetpea’s second season finds its footing in a chaotic murder plot
content.shortHeadline: Sweetpea improves when it embraces the chaos
content.standfirst: Ella Purnell returns as Rhiannon, a meek journalist who murders men, in a season the Guardian still finds uneven. A copycat killer and a larger ensemble give the series more momentum, even as its feminist-revenge premise remains unsettled.

image.caption: Ella Purnell as Rhiannon in season two of Sweetpea.

sources.originalTitle: Sweetpea review – why was this disastrous serial killer comedy even given a second chance?

segments.body: Sweetpea returns with Rhiannon hiding a boyfriend’s body in her freezer and dealing with the guilt of having killed a blameless man in the previous season. The Guardian’s review recalls how the first run struggled to reconcile its everyday coming-of-age concerns with the violence of a vigilante-killer story.

segments.title: A wider cast, a messier story
segments.body: The new season adds a dynamic editor, a grieving mother and a doctor who treats Rhiannon’s recurring nosebleeds. When a copycat killer begins targeting men, the plot gains fresh momentum. The review says the show is more enjoyable when it stops pretending to be a coherent feminist-revenge story and leans into its eccentric, fast-moving chaos.

content.headline: Alan Carr’s Great Big Bucket List makes opting out its great pleasure
content.shortHeadline: Alan Carr’s comfort-first adventure show
content.standfirst: Carr tries activities with celebrity friends but does not have to finish anything he dislikes. The Guardian finds the lack of jeopardy—alongside his attempts at flying, bungee jumping and less intimidating outings—an unexpectedly soothing formula.

image.caption: Alan Carr and Mel Giedroyc in Alan Carr’s Great Big Bucket List.

sources.originalTitle: Alan Carr’s Great Big Bucket List review – the comfort show of my happiest dreams

segments.body: In Alan Carr’s Great Big Bucket List, the comedian attempts experiences with celebrity companions, including learning to fly a loop-the-loop with Mel Giedroyc and considering a bungee jump with Joanne McNally. The Guardian’s reviewer loves the premise that Carr can refuse any activity he does not want to complete.

segments.title: The appeal of no pressure
segments.body: Carr declines to take the controls of the plane and balks at other challenges, while still trying gentler pursuits such as driving a steam train, seeing a waterfall and going whale watching. The review argues that watching him opt out is more relaxing than the usual reality-TV tension of a celebrity being pushed past their limits.

segments.title: Company counts
segments.body: The programme’s pleasure also comes from Carr’s easy rapport with friends: the review highlights jokes about luxury-car airbags, an attempted interruption at a wedding and McNally’s own hesitation before a jump. Its verdict is uncomplicated: the half-hours are charming, funny and deliberately low-stakes.

content.headline: The Hunting Wives turns Texas culture-war politics into glossy soap
content.shortHeadline: The Hunting Wives plays both sides of Texas politics
content.standfirst: Netflix’s steamy drama returns to an affluent east Texas community of secrets and political divides. The BBC finds its satire of both liberal and conservative characters, and its focus on female pleasure, central to the show’s appeal.

sources.originalTitle: 'It appeals across demographics': How steamy soap The Hunting Wives took on sex, scandal and the US's blue-red divide

segments.body: The Hunting Wives follows Sophie, an East Coast political communications professional, and Margo, the wife of a Texas oil tycoon, as their affair develops amid a wealthy community’s secrets. The BBC says the show’s first season drew a large Netflix audience; the second, released on 26 November, brings more scandal and a murder investigation.

segments.title: Satire without a side
segments.body: The series makes fun of both the Republican elite and its Democrat-leaning newcomers. The BBC quotes TV critic Judy Berman, who argues that the characters’ focus on optics over ethics lets the drama satirise politics as performance rather than take a direct position on partisan issues.

perspectives.body: Texas Monthly editor Taylor Prewitt says the show’s cross-aisle teasing reflects the state’s varied politics, where people with opposing views often have to interact.

segments.title: The female gaze
segments.body: The BBC also highlights the series’ depiction of female pleasure, including scenes that are unusual for a mainstream glossy soap. Star Malin Åkerman says the show’s female creator, showrunner and directors helped shape its perspective on what women find sexy and beautiful.

content.headline: I’m a Celebrity’s “aggressive” label for AJ Odudu revives a familiar stereotype
content.shortHeadline: AJ Odudu and the “aggressive” label on I’m a Celebrity
content.standfirst: The i argues that journalist Mariella Frostrup’s description of presenter AJ Odudu on I’m a Celebrity reflects a recurring stereotype faced by Black women. Campmates disagreed with Frostrup, and producers reportedly spoke to her about the language.

image.caption: AJ Odudu on I’m a Celebrity… Get Me Out of Here!

sources.originalTitle: Mariella Frostrup’s behaviour is all too familiar to Black women like me

segments.body: After AJ Odudu questioned Mariella Frostrup’s claim to be pleased about help with cooking, Frostrup called Odudu “aggressive”. The i’s writer says the exchange looked different on screen: Odudu spoke softly, while Frostrup raised her voice, and the writer sees the label as part of a familiar pattern of Black women being treated as aggressive for reasonable behaviour.

segments.title: A disagreement in camp
segments.body: Wayne Rooney and Claire Sweeney, who saw the exchange, told Frostrup they did not think Odudu had been aggressive. The article says the two later attempted to clear the air, but Frostrup did not retract the word. Producers have reportedly spoken to her about her language; the piece notes that the impact on Odudu may outlast the argument itself.

content.headline: Grand Theft Auto VI makes routine and romance part of its criminal world
content.shortHeadline: GTA VI finds tenderness in the everyday
content.standfirst: The vast game can move from shootouts to grocery shopping, workouts and caring for a pet snake. The Guardian’s review finds new emotional weight in Jason and Lucia’s relationship, while a separate essay argues that routine is part of the game’s pleasure.

image.caption: Jason and Lucia, the fugitive couple at the centre of Grand Theft Auto VI.

sources.originalTitle: Grand Theft Auto VI review – gaming’s most depraved world is now also its greatest love story
The unexpected joy hiding in Grand Theft Auto VI’s chaos? A little routine

segments.body: The Guardian’s review describes Grand Theft Auto VI as an enormous, detailed world that accommodates both high-speed crime and ordinary activities, from shopping to assembling furniture. At its centre are Jason and Lucia, a fugitive couple whose attempts to build a life together give the game an emotional anchor.

segments.title: The pleasure of keeping things going
segments.body: A separate Guardian account focuses on Jason’s daily routine: getting dressed, working out, feeding his pet snake and handling errands. It argues that GTA VI makes tasks familiar from everyday life pleasurable through the game’s tactile world and the relationship between the characters.

perspectives.body: The routine-focused piece argues that games often revolve around tidying, checklists and repeated tasks; GTA VI makes those rhythms appealing by connecting them to care for someone else.

segments.title: A different kind of GTA
segments.body: The main review sees the series’ familiar vulgarity and violent chaos alongside a new invitation to empathise. It says Lucia, the first female protagonist, changes how the game’s treatment of women lands, while noting the game remains deliberately offensive and has firmly earned its adult rating.

content.headline: Independent developers bring GTA-style chaos to their own cities
content.shortHeadline: Small studios make open-world crime games their own
content.standfirst: From a Manchester estate to 1970s Istanbul, independent developers are adapting the open-world template to places they know. Their games trade blockbuster scale for local detail, distinct settings and, in one case, a gentler take on crime.

image.caption: A scene from The Estate, set on a Manchester council estate.

sources.originalTitle: GTA in Istanbul? Meet the game developers bringing virtual crime chaos to their home cities

segments.body: The Guardian meets developers making open-world games in the spirit of Grand Theft Auto. Eamonn Swayah’s The Estate is set on a Manchester council estate, while Burak Akşahin’s Alaturka takes players to 1970s Istanbul. Both draw on places and cultural details rarely seen in blockbuster crime games.

segments.title: Local settings, different ambitions
segments.body: The Estate uses low-poly graphics, Mancunian radio chat and small-scale thefts to build its own sense of place. Akşahin’s game includes kebab-shop minigames and an Anatolian soundtrack, following a newcomer who hopes to earn enough to return to his village and marry.

segments.title: Beyond the copycat
segments.body: The article also describes Helsinki Online, a browser-based city sandbox whose creator has deliberately limited crime, and Last Drop, a darker Finnish game informed by stories of alcoholism. The developers see the influence of GTA as a starting point, not a requirement to reproduce its scale or approach.

content.headline: Grand Theft Auto VI’s soundtrack brings a star-studded new set of songs
content.shortHeadline: GTA VI’s album brings new music to Vice City
content.standfirst: Justice, Dua Lipa, Travis Scott and Latin artists feature on an album of new material tied to the game. The Guardian review sees the soundtrack as a showcase for Rockstar’s cultural reach and taste, with a few tracks that miss.

image.caption: Justice, who composed music for Grand Theft Auto VI and contributed to its soundtrack album.

sources.originalTitle: Grand Theft Auto VI: The Album review – even GTA sceptics will warm to this zeitgeisty, star-packed soundtrack

segments.body: The soundtrack album for Grand Theft Auto VI collects new songs from artists including Justice, Dua Lipa, Travis Scott, Cardi B and Rauw Alejandro. Justice’s “Starting from Zero”, featuring Doobie Brothers singer Michael McDonald, opens with an ’80s-style pop ballad that nods to Vice City’s setting.

segments.title: A global radio dial
segments.body: The game itself contains 22 radio stations and 700 licensed songs across nine decades. The review highlights the breadth of the in-game music, from club-focused artists such as Arca and Rina Sawayama to the dreamy “Largate” by Helado Negro and Kali Uchis, while noting that the album is only a small part of what players will hear.

segments.title: A cultural platform
